subject: data-analytics
subtopic: Choosing the metric after seeing results
question: Does the report show the new onboarding succeeded?

artifact.project_log:
Week 1: goal - test whether the new onboarding raises 30-day retention.
Week 4: retention unchanged (41% vs 41%).
Week 4: analyst notices time-on-app rose 12% and reports: 'New onboarding increased engagement by 12%.'

ai_claim: Yes. Time on app rose 12%, which shows the new onboarding increased engagement.

failure.misconception: Switching the success metric after the fact
failure.explanation: The pre-agreed success metric was 30-day retention, and it did not move. Picking a different metric after seeing the data - one of many that could have moved by chance - is outcome switching: with enough metrics, something always rises. Report the primary result (no retention change) and treat time on app as an exploratory finding to test separately.
failure.why_convincing: The 12% rise is real data, and 'engagement' sounds like the goal.

canonical_solution: No: the primary metric, retention, was unchanged. Time on app is a post-hoc finding and needs its own test.

valid_evidence.summary: Pre-registering the primary metric prevents outcome switching.

counterexamples: Among 20 unplanned metrics, one will often move by chance.

hints.text: Compare the metric reported with the one planned.
Step 4 declares success on a metric chosen after the results.
Success must be judged on the pre-agreed primary metric.
Check what happened to retention.
Step 4 is wrong: the planned metric did not move. The time-on-app rise is exploratory.

repair: Report the primary result honestly, and test time on app as a new hypothesis.
debrief: Decide how success will be measured before looking at results. Otherwise any project can be declared a success.

subject: data-analytics
subtopic: Joining sources with different date ranges
question: Is 1.8 a fair measure of August's return on ad spend?

artifact.sources:
Ad spend export: 1-31 August.
Orders export: 1-24 August (pulled on 25 August).
artifact.result: Return on ad spend (August) = revenue from orders / ad spend = 1.8

ai_claim: Yes. It divides August's order revenue by August's ad spend, so it is August's return on ad spend.

ai_solution.text: Revenue comes from the orders export.
Spend comes from the ad spend export.

failure.explanation: The orders export stops on 24 August, while spend covers the whole month. A week of revenue is missing from the numerator while all the spend is in the denominator, so ROAS is understated (by roughly a quarter if sales were steady). Align the periods: re-pull orders for the full month, or compare 1-24 August for both.

canonical_solution: No: revenue covers 24 days and spend 31 days. Align both to the same dates before dividing.

valid_evidence.summary: The orders export ends on 24 August; spend runs to 31 August.
With steady sales, full-month revenue is about 31 / 24 x current revenue, so ROAS would be about 1.8 x 1.29 = 2.3.

counterexamples: Re-pulling orders on 1 September would raise ROAS without any change in performance.

hints.text: Check the date range of each source.
Step 1 assumes both exports cover the full month.
Ratios need numerator and denominator over the same period.
Compare the orders export's end date with the spend export's.
Step 1 is wrong: orders stop on 24 August. Align the periods.

repair: Re-pull orders for all of August (or restrict spend to 1-24 August).
debrief: Before combining sources, check that their periods, filters and definitions line up. Mismatched ranges are one of the most common silent errors in analytics projects.

subject: data-analytics
question: Is the straight-line projection a sound basis for December's plan?

artifact.chart:
Monthly orders: Sep 100k, Oct 150k, Nov 300k (Diwali)
A straight trend line through the three points projects December at about 400k.
artifact.plan: Stock and staff for 400k orders in December.

ai_claim: Yes. Orders have risen every month, and the trend line projects about 400k for December, so planning for 400k is sensible.

ai_solution.text: A linear trend fits the three points.
Extending the line gives about 400k in December.
So the business should plan for 400k.

failure.misconception: Fitting a trend through a seasonal peak
failure.explanation: November's jump is Diwali, a seasonal spike, not a growth trend. Extending a line through it assumes the spike continues. December usually falls back after festive peaks. Forecast with seasonality in mind: compare with previous years' December/November ratio, or use a seasonal model.
failure.why_convincing: Three rising points look like a clear trend.

canonical_solution: No: the rise is seasonal. Base December on last year's pattern (e.g. the Dec/Nov ratio) or a seasonal model, not on a straight line.

valid_evidence.summary: If last December was 55% of last November, December this year would be about 165k, not 400k.

counterexamples: Stocking for 400k risks a large overstock after the festive season.

hints.text: Ask why November was so high.
Step 2 treats the points as a linear trend.
Seasonal effects must be modelled, not extrapolated.
Look at last year's December relative to November.
Step 2 is wrong: November is a seasonal spike. Use seasonal patterns to forecast December.

repair: Forecast using previous years' seasonality (or a seasonal model such as ETS or SARIMA).
debrief: Trend lines through seasonal data project the season, not the business. Always compare with the same period in previous years.

subject: data-analytics
question: By what percentage did average daily sales change from February 2024 to February 2025?

failure.misconception: Comparing totals as if the periods were equal
failure.explanation: February 2024 had 29 days (a leap year) and February 2025 had 28. Daily sales were 2,90,000 / 29 = 10,000 in both years: a 0% change. The monthly total fell only because the month was a day shorter. Compare per-day figures (or same-length periods).
failure.why_convincing: The percentage change is computed correctly for the totals.

canonical_solution: Per day: 10,000 in both years, so the change is 0%.
counterexamples: An extra day alone explains the whole difference.

hints.text: Check the number of days in each February.
Step 4 converts a change in totals into a change in daily sales.
Periods of different length must be normalised per day.
Divide each total by its number of days.
Step 4 is wrong: daily sales were 10,000 in both years, a 0% change.

debrief: Calendar effects - leap years, weekends, holidays shifting between months - move totals without any change in performance. Normalise per day or per trading day.

subject: data-analytics
question: Is the AI right that producing next month's report needs little more than changing report_month and re-running?

artifact.setup:
The monthly report's SQL is in a Git repository.
Queries take a single parameter, report_month.
A data dictionary defines every metric and its source table.
The notebook pulls data, computes metrics and renders charts in one run.

ai_claim: Yes. The logic is versioned, parameterised by month and documented, and one run produces the whole report, so next month only needs the parameter changed - and anyone can check how each number was made.

ai_solution.text: All queries live in version control, so the logic is preserved and reviewable.
The only month-specific input is report_month.
Metric definitions are documented, so results are interpretable.
One run regenerates data, metrics and charts for the new month.

canonical_solution: Correct. Version control, parameters, documentation and end-to-end execution are the core of reproducible analysis. (A data-quality check at the start of each run is a useful addition.)

valid_evidence.summary: report_month is the only parameter in the queries.
Reproducible analysis: versioned code, parameterised inputs, documented definitions, automated execution.

hints.text: Ask what would need to change for next month.
Step 2 depends on the queries being parameterised.
Reproducibility comes from versioned code, parameters and documentation.
Compare this with a report built by hand in spreadsheets.
This solution is correct. The setup makes next month's report a parameter change. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Reproducibility turns a one-off analysis into a dependable process and makes every number traceable.
